title: The Case for Seeking Early Commitment
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Effective leaders gain commitment to the overall direction of a proposal before negotiating the details of implementation. When people agree on the destination first, they develop psychological ownership that sustains them through the friction of the messy middle. Early commitment inhibits people from rejecting an entire path forward merely because of how it will be executed. Separating strategy from tactics prevents discarding a sound direction over implementation disagreements. Research supports that gaining early commitment to a direction actually improves implementation quality. Leaders must, however, strengthen the proposal before seeking commitment, and they should naturally revisit that commitment if new information surfaces that exposes a flaw in the plan.
points: * Committing to direction first and refining execution later makes people more flexible when collaborating on the details. * Early commitment creates psychological ownership: people who agree to a direction early invest more creative energy in making the work succeed. * Good leaders separate strategy from tactics -- they offer the big picture to gain commitment, knowing the details must still be negotiated. * Early commitment reduces drift, delay, and ambiguity, but only if the underlying plan is sound -- weak plans produce equally subpar execution decisions. * Leaders should revisit commitment when serious new information suggests the plan is flawed; commitment is not a trap.
quotes: When people agree to the goal up front, they are more likely to push through the messy middle when friction ensues, rather than complain or delay.

Good leaders don't seek early commitment as a trap to close the deal before surfacing the details. Instead, they offer the big picture behind the idea or goal, thus gaining commitment to the overall direction.

Early commitment to the idea inhibits people from rejecting the path forward because of how it will be executed. Research does suggest that gaining early commitment to a direction actually improves implementation.
Evidence favors committing people early to the direction while preserving the flexibility to determine how to execute the plan later. This creates buy-in and ownership for team members.
